subject: Biology
title: Seals, Sea Lions, and Walruses
description: A quick win: understand Seals, Sea Lions, and Walruses.

hook.text: Pinnipeds live in two worlds—hunting in the sea and breeding on land. They mastered both.

buildup.text: Seals swim with rear flippers and can't walk on land. Sea lions use all four flippers to walk.

discovery.text: Elephant seal males can weigh 2,300 kg and dive to 1,500 meters—holding breath for 2 hours.

twist.text: Walruses use their tusks as ice picks to haul themselves out of the water—not primarily as weapons.

climax.text: Arctic pinnipeds are losing sea ice habitat faster than they can adapt to warming temperatures.

punchline.text: Masters of land and sea—if there's still ice to rest on.

quiz.question: How long can an elephant seal hold its breath?

details.summary: Pinnipeds, including seals, sea lions, and walruses, are marine mammals that split their time between ocean and shore. They evolved from bear-like ancestors about 50 million years ago and developed streamlined bodies, powerful flippers, and diving physiology for aquatic hunting.
details.whyItMatters: Pinnipeds are indicators of ocean health and key members of marine food webs. Their populations were devastated by historical hunting. Recovery of some species shows conservation success while others remain endangered from climate change.
takeaways: True seals swim with rear flippers while sea lions use front flippers
Weddell seals can dive to 600 meters and hold breath for over 80 minutes
Walrus tusks are enlarged canine teeth used for hauling out onto ice

faq.question: What is the difference between seals and sea lions?
faq.answer: Sea lions have external ear flaps, can rotate their rear flippers forward to walk on land, and swim using front flippers. True seals lack external ears, cannot rotate rear flippers, move on land by belly-flopping, and swim using side-to-side rear flipper movement.

faq.question: How are pinnipeds affected by climate change?
faq.answer: Arctic and Antarctic species like walruses, ringed seals, and leopard seals depend on sea ice for resting, breeding, and pup-rearing. Shrinking ice forces longer swims and increased competition. Walruses crowding onto beaches due to ice loss causes deadly stampedes.
